#Today

- Shape Integration  
- Modularity  
- Multivariate Evolutionary Rates  
- + Phylogenetic PCA (^)

---
# Big Picture
.pull-left[


Today we’ll connect four ideas:

- **Integration**: traits covary → “things move together”
- **Modularity**: covariance is **blocky** → semi-independent parts
- **Multivariate rates**: how fast **shape as a vector** evolves
- **Phylogenetic PCA**: PCA that accounts for shared ancestry

**Unifying theme:** covariance structure.
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S0047248422000914-gr1.jpg" width="500">

]

---

# Step 1: What is Integration?

.pull-left[


Imagine measuring:

- Jaw length
- Head width
- Eye size
- Body depth

If these tend to change together → **integrated**.

If they vary independently → weak integration.

**Integration = structure in covariance** (not just “correlation”).
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://res.cloudinary.com/dry8rzbyx/image/fetch/s--YSWEWrj9--/f_auto/q_auto/c_scale,w_1536/https://www.knime.com/sites/default/files/public/9-descriptive-statistics-knime.png" width="500">

]

---
# Visual Intuition

.pull-left[


Two traits:

- Integrated → tight diagonal cloud (predictable)
- Not integrated → round cloud (independent-ish)

If you can predict trait B from trait A, there’s integration.
]

.pull-right[
<img src="https://res.cloudinary.com/dry8rzbyx/image/fetch/s--YSWEWrj9--/f_auto/q_auto/c_scale,w_1536/https://www.knime.com/sites/default/files/public/9-descriptive-statistics-knime.png" width="500">

]

---
# Why Does Integration Exist?
.pull-left[


Three common causes:

1. **Developmental coupling** (shared pathways)
2. **Functional coupling** (works together)
3. **Genetic correlations** (shared genetic basis)

]

.pull-right[
<img src="https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S0047248422000914-gr1.jpg" width="500">
]

---
# Translation to Matrices

.pull-left[

Integration lives in the covariance matrix:

- Strong integration → large off-diagonals, variation concentrated
- Weak integration → covariance spread more evenly

Think: “Is there a dominant direction of variation?”
]

.pull-right[
```{r,echo=F,message=F,warning=F}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)
library(tidyverse)
})
# -----------------------------
# 1. Define covariance matrices
# -----------------------------

traits <- c("Jaw", "Head", "Body")

low_cov <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.05, 0.02,
  0.05, 1.0, 0.03,
  0.02, 0.03, 1.0
), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

medium_cov <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.4, 0.3,
  0.4, 1.0, 0.35,
  0.3, 0.35, 1.0
), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

high_cov <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.8, 0.75,
  0.8, 1.0, 0.85,
  0.75, 0.85, 1.0
), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# Add row/column names
for (mat in list(low_cov, medium_cov, high_cov)) {
  colnames(mat) <- rownames(mat) <- traits
}

# -----------------------------
# 2. Convert to tidy dataframe
# -----------------------------

make_df <- function(mat, level){
  as.data.frame(as.table(mat)) %>%
    rename(Trait1 = Var1,
           Trait2 = Var2,
           Covariance = Freq) %>%
    mutate(Integration = level)
}

df_low    <- make_df(low_cov, "Low")
df_medium <- make_df(medium_cov, "Medium")
df_high   <- make_df(high_cov, "High")

df_all <- bind_rows(df_low, df_medium, df_high)

# -----------------------------
# 3. Plot heatmaps
# -----------------------------

ggplot(df_all, aes(Trait1, Trait2, fill = Covariance)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0.5,
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Integration) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(title = "Low vs Medium vs High Integration",
       fill = "Covariance")
```
]

---
# Eigenvectors = Directions of Shape Change

.pull-left[

PCA is an eigen-decomposition of covariance.

If **PC1 explains a lot**, variation is “channeled” → stronger integration.

If variance is evenly spread across many PCs → weaker integration.
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://www.sthda.com/sthda/RDoc/figure/factor-analysis/factominer-principal-component-analysis-eigenvalue-factoextra-data-mining-1.png" width="500">

]

---
# Modularity




---
# What is Modularity?

.pull-left[


A **module** = traits that:

- covary strongly **within** the group
- covary weakly **between** groups

Classic examples:
- face vs braincase
- fin modules (pectoral vs caudal)
- jaw joint vs tooth-bearing region
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-018-25715-y/MediaObjects/41598_2018_25715_Fig2_HTML.jpg" width="400">

]

---
# What Modularity Looks Like

.pull-left[


Covariance matrix becomes “blocky”:

<table style="border-collapse: collapse; font-family: monospace; text-align: center;">
  <tr>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">A</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">A</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">A</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">A</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">B</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">B</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">0</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">B</td>
    <td style="border: 1px solid #333; padding: 6px;">B</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Strong within-module covariance, weak across modules.
]

.pull-right[
```{r,echo=F}
traits <- c("M1_T1","M1_T2","M2_T1","M2_T2")

# Block covariance: strong within-module (A and B), weak between modules (0)
C_block <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.8, 0.05, 0.05,
  0.8, 1.0, 0.05, 0.05,
  0.05, 0.05, 1.0, 0.8,
  0.05, 0.05, 0.8, 1.0
), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

colnames(C_block) <- rownames(C_block) <- traits

df <- as.data.frame(as.table(C_block)) %>%
  rename(Trait1 = Var1, Trait2 = Var2, Covariance = Freq)

ggplot(df, aes(Trait1, Trait2, fill = Covariance)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "Block-structured covariance (two modules)") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1))
```
]

---
# Why Modularity Matters

.pull-left[


Modularity can increase **evolvability** because:

- selection can change one module without dragging everything else
- local adaptation becomes easier
- constraints can be localized

Key idea: modularity = semi-independence.
]

.pull-right[

]

---

.pull-left[
# Testing Modularity (Intuition)

We ask:

- Is within-module covariance > between-module covariance?

Common tests/metrics:
- RV coefficient
- Covariance ratio (CR)
- permutation/random-partition comparisons

You need a **hypothesis of modules** (a partition).
]

.pull-right[
<img src="https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-018-25715-y/MediaObjects/41598_2018_25715_Fig2_HTML.jpg" width="400">
]

---
# Integration vs Modularity
.pull-left[

They are not opposites.

You can have:
- strong integration **within** modules
- weak integration **between** modules

That’s structured integration (often what biology looks like).
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://damelo.net/publication/modularityandintegration/featured.jpg"  width="400" >


]

# Multivariate Evolutionary Rates

---
# Univariate Rate Reminder

.pull-left[


Brownian motion (BM):
- trait variance increases linearly with time
- rate parameter: **σ²**

Univariate question:
“How fast does trait X evolve?”
]

.pull-right[
<!-- Add a time vs variance sketch -->

<img src="https://lukejharmon.github.io/pcm/images/figure3-1.png"  width="400" >

]

---
# Multivariate Rate Idea
.pull-left[


Now traits form a vector:

**shape = (x1, x2, …, xp)**

Question becomes:
“How fast does the *shape vector* diffuse through morphospace?”
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-018-25715-y/MediaObjects/41598_2018_25715_Fig1_HTML.jpg"  width="400" >

]

---
# The Evolutionary Rate Matrix (R)
.pull-left[


Under multivariate BM, rate is a matrix:

- diagonals = per-trait rates
- off-diagonals = evolutionary covariances

Interpretation:
- big eigenvalues → fast along major axes
- small eigenvalues → slow / constrained axes

* λ1 = 1.8 → fast evolution along major axis
* λ2 = 0.2 → slow evolution orthogonal to that
]

.pull-right[
```{r}
R <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.8,
  0.8, 1.0
), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

R
eigen(R)

```


]


---
# The Evolutionary Rate Matrix (R)

.pull-left[
* λ1 = 1.8 → fast evolution along major axis
* λ2 = 0.2 → slow evolution orthogonal to that

```{r,warning=F,message=F}
library(MASS)
set.seed(1)
sim_data <- mvrnorm(n = 1000, 
                    mu = c(0,0), 
                    Sigma = R)
```

]

.pull-right[
```{r,warning=F,message=F}
plot(sim_data,
     pch = 16,
     col = rgb(0,0,1,0.3),
     asp = 1,
     main = "Evolutionary diffusion under R")
```

**That ellipse is the eigenstructure of R**

]

---
# The Evolutionary Rate Matrix (R)

.pull-left[
* λ1 = 1 → fast evolution along major axis
* λ2 = 1 → fast evolution orthogonal to that

```{r,warning=F,message=F,fig.height=2}
R2 <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.0,
  0.0, 1.0
), nrow = 2)

eigen(R2)
set.seed(1)

sim_data2 <- mvrnorm(n = 1000, 
                    mu = c(0,0), 
                    Sigma = R2)
```

]

.pull-right[
```{r,warning=F,message=F}
plot(sim_data2,
     pch = 16,
     col = rgb(0,0,1,0.3),
     asp = 1,
     main = "Evolutionary diffusion under R")
```


]


---

.pull-left[
# Rate vs Integration

Strong integration does **not** automatically mean slow evolution.

It can mean:
- evolution is *channeled* along certain axes
- constrained in others

So you can see:
- high rate along PC1-like axis
- low rate orthogonal to it
]

.pull-right[
```{r}
plot(sim_data,
     pch = 16,
     col = rgb(0,0,1,0.3),
     asp = 1,
     main = "Evolutionary diffusion under R")
```
]

# Phylogenetic PCA (pPCA)

---
# Why PCA Can Mislead
.pull-left[


Regular PCA treats species as independent.

But species share history, so raw covariance includes:
- evolutionary signal (shared ancestry)
- plus whatever ecology/selection adds

So PCA axes can reflect phylogeny as much as “functional structure”.
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-018-25715-y/MediaObjects/41598_2018_25715_Fig1_HTML.jpg?as=webp"  width="400" >

]

---
# What pPCA Tries to Do

.pull-left[


Phylogenetic PCA adjusts for expected covariance under a phylogenetic model
(usually BM) before doing PCA.

Goal:
- describe major axes of variation **after accounting for shared ancestry**
- interpret PCs as “phylogenetically informed” shape axes
]

.pull-right[
**Same concept, different pile**
]

---
# Two Common Flavors
.pull-left[


1) **pPCA via BM-transformed covariance**
   - estimate phylogenetic covariance among species
   - transform data → do PCA

2) **PGLS-style residual PCA**
   - regress traits on intercept with phylogenetic error (BM)
   - PCA on residuals / transformed data

Both are trying to reduce the “non-independence problem.”
]

.pull-right[
<!-- Add an algorithm schematic -->
]

---
# How to Interpret pPC Axes
.pull-left[


pPC1 is still:
- a direction of major variation in the dataset

But now it’s major variation *given the phylogeny/model*.

Practical interpretation:
- pPCs often emphasize shifts that are **not just deep clade structure**
- sometimes axes rotate compared to ordinary PCA
]


---
# PCA vs pPCA 

```{r,echo=F,warning=F,message=F,fig.height=4}
# ---------------------------------
# 1. Load packages
# ---------------------------------
library(ape)
library(phytools)

set.seed(123)

# ---------------------------------
# 2. Simulate phylogeny
# ---------------------------------
tree <- rtree(60)

# ---------------------------------
# 3. Simulate 2 traits under BM
# ---------------------------------
R <- matrix(c(
  1.0, 0.7,
  0.7, 1.0
), 2, 2)

X <- fastBM(tree, nsim = 2, sig2 = 1)
X <- as.matrix(X)

# ---------------------------------
# 4. Add a clade-level shift
# ---------------------------------
# Pick a large clade
clade_node <- getMRCA(tree, tree$tip.label[1:30])
clade_tips <- extract.clade(tree, clade_node)$tip.label

# Add a mean shift to that clade
X[clade_tips, ] <- X[clade_tips, ] + c(4, 4)

# ---------------------------------
# 5. Regular PCA
# ---------------------------------
pca <- prcomp(X, scale. = FALSE)

# ---------------------------------
# 6. Phylogenetic PCA
# ---------------------------------
ppca <- phyl.pca(tree, X, method = "BM")

# ---------------------------------
# 7. Plot side by side
# ---------------------------------
par(mfrow = c(1,2))

plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2],
     pch = 16,
     col = "steelblue",
     main = "Regular PCA",
     xlab = "PC1",
     ylab = "PC2")

plot(ppca$S[,1], ppca$S[,2],
     pch = 16,
     col = "firebrick",
     main = "Phylogenetic PCA",
     xlab = "pPC1",
     ylab = "pPC2")
```

---

.pull-left[
# Important Caveat

pPCA depends on the assumed evolutionary model.

If the real process deviates strongly from BM:
- pPCA can “overcorrect” or distort
- interpretation changes

Best practice:
- compare PCA and pPCA
- check phylogenetic signal
- be explicit about model assumptions
]
